name: Unscented products for natural scent
lead: Using unscented or fragrance-free products is a grooming practice in which people choose soaps, deodorants and lotions without added fragrance, so that their own skin scent is not mixed with or overwhelmed by a perfume or cologne. People do it to smell clean and natural, avoid a clash between product scents and a chosen fragrance, and, in appearance communities, to let natural body scent do its work in attraction.

The practice overlaps with the skin-scent theory of attraction and with a more general interest in avoiding fragrance allergens. Fragrance contact allergy is a recognized condition, and it is one common reason for choosing fragranced-free products in dermatology.[1]
infobox: Avoid fragrance clash; keep natural scent
Natural body odor and immune-gene (MHC) compatibility [2]

paras: Deodorants lower odor with alcohol, antibacterial agents and perfumes that mask smell, while antiperspirants block sweat pores to reduce sweat. Many conventional versions are scented.[2] Practitioners of the unscented approach choose versions without added perfume, and often fragrance-free laundry and body-care products, and may rely on washing to control odor.
Wikipedia notes that daily bathing with antibacterial soap reduces skin bacteria, and that deodorant or antiperspirant use after bathing may further reduce odor.[2]

About 10 percent of patients with eczema react to a standard fragrance mix on patch testing, and consumer products use about 2,500 fragrance ingredients, roughly 100 of which are known to cause reactions in some people.[1] Reported symptoms include allergic contact dermatitis, headaches and asthma attacks.[1]

Two US surveys cited on Wikipedia found that 30.5 percent of respondents were irritated by scented products on other people.[1] The article also notes that products labeled fragrance-free may still contain less recognizable fragrance chemicals.[1]

The practice is tied to claims that natural body odor carries information, such as immune-gene (MHC) compatibility, and that women tend to prefer different MHC types in male odor.[2] Whether leaving off perfume improves attractiveness has not been tested directly, and the role of human pheromones remains disputed.[2]
No studies found comparing the attractiveness of people using unscented versus scented grooming products. Studies of fragrance sensitivity in general are noted above.[1]

card.summary: Fragrance-free grooming so your own smell isn't clashing with cologne; attraction benefit is untested, allergy reasons are documented.
card.note: Fragrance-free labels can still include lesser-known fragrance chemicals.

quick.overview:
People using this approach pick soaps, deodorants and lotions without added fragrance so their natural scent is not masked or clashing with a cologne.

Skin reactions to fragrance are well documented, but no studies have tested whether going unscented makes someone more attractive.
quick.mechanism: Removing added perfume leaves skin scent shaped by bacteria, gland secretions and washing habits. Deodorants and antiperspirants without perfume still reduce odor or sweat.
quick.risks: Few risks are reported. Products labeled fragrance-free can still include less-known fragrance chemicals, and unscented products may not control odor for everyone.

chain: Own skin scent is not masked or clashed
angle.text: Wearers pick unscented grooming products so their natural scent, or a single chosen cologne, comes through cleanly. Some also choose fragrance-free products to avoid skin reactions.
